passage:
It was past one in the morning in the hostel common room, and Tanuja was still scrolling. A flood somewhere. A crash on the highway. A thread about how every job would vanish in five years. A video of a fight outside a shopping centre. Each post pulled her to the next.
Zeenat, coming back from the washroom, saw the blue glow. "Still up?"
"Everything is getting worse," Tanuja said, not looking up. "Like, everything. I don't even know why I'm studying."
"What did you actually learn tonight that you didn't know at ten?"
Tanuja opened her mouth, then closed it. Her chest was tight, her tea was cold, and she couldn't name one new fact.
"Phone in my locker till morning?" Zeenat offered. Tanuja hesitated, then handed it over.

qa.q: What time was it in the hostel common room?
qa.a: Past one in the morning.

qa.q: Why does Tanuja feel that everything is getting worse?
qa.a: She has seen bad post after bad post for hours, so the world starts to feel like nothing but floods, crashes and fights, and her worry grows with each one. 😰

qa.q: Which step helped, and what could Tanuja do on other nights?
qa.a: Handing the phone to Zeenat broke the loop; on other nights she could set a time to stop and check news once a day from a calm source.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat to find Tanuja scrolling at one in the morning?
qa.a: Zeenat seems worried and wants to help without lecturing, so Zeenat asks a simple question and offers to keep the phone.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking bad news late into the night, growing more distressed while learning nothing new.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
Sorry I missed your call on Sunday. I've been in a strange mood. Every night I tell myself I'll read the news for five minutes, and then it's two hours of break-ins, accidents, angry posts and videos of people shouting at each other. Last night I read about three chain-snatchings in our city, and today I didn't want to take the metro to college. I went, of course. Nothing happened. Nobody even looked at me.
It just feels like the world has become so much worse than when we were kids. Everyone online says so. But when I try to say what has actually changed, I can't. I only know I feel worse.
Do you feel this too, over there?
Love,
Salma

qa.q: How many chain-snatchings did Salma read about last night?
qa.a: Three chain-snatchings in their city.

qa.q: Why does Salma feel the world has become so much worse?
qa.a: Salma feels anxious after hours of bad news every night, with everyone online agreeing, so the fear seems like fact even though Salma can't name what has changed.

qa.q: What could Salma try instead of reading for two hours?
qa.a: Set a short, fixed time for news, stop well before bed, and count real days like the calm metro ride as evidence too.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel reading this email?
qa.a: Elizabeth might be worried about Salma's mood and want to gently point out that the metro ride went fine.

grounding: It shows a young adult reading bad news for hours and concluding the world is worse, while fear grows and real information does not.

passage: For the campus radio's Honest Hour, this is Lakshmi. Last semester I got hooked on bad news. It started with one cyclone update. Then I'd wake at 3 a.m. and check: more storms, a bridge collapse, a post saying our generation has no future, a thread about layoffs. Every refresh felt like keeping watch, as if something would sneak up on me if I stopped. My roommate Sangeeta would ask, "Anything new?" and honestly, most nights, no. Same stories, new angry comments. But my heart would be racing and I'd skip breakfast. I told Sangeeta the world was ending. She asked what I'd do differently if it was. I had no answer. I just knew I felt terrible, and scrolling didn't make me know any more.

qa.q: At what time would Lakshmi wake up and check the news?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: Why did scrolling feel like "keeping watch" to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt anxious that stopping would let something bad sneak up, so each refresh felt like protection and the checking felt necessary even though it brought no new information.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi have done on those 3 a.m. nights?
qa.a: Keep the phone out of reach at night, and if the worry stays heavy, talk to Sangeeta or the college counsellor.

qa.q: What was it like for Sangeeta to share a room with Lakshmi then?
qa.a: Sangeeta likely saw the racing heart and skipped breakfasts and felt worried, asking gentle questions to help Lakshmi notice nothing new was being learned.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking bad news at night, feeling the world is ending while gaining no real information.

passage:
I'm Chandrika. My sister Amandeep, nineteen, came with us to Nani's house in Shimla for the winter break, and I spent most of it watching the top of her head.
She scrolled at breakfast: a fire somewhere, a scam, an angry thread. She scrolled on the walk to the Mall Road and walked into a lamp post. On the second night it snowed for the first time in years. Nani and I were at the window shouting for her. She came, looked for a second, then went back to a video about some crime.
At dinner she said, "Honestly, the world is getting worse every day. It's all falling apart." Nani asked what had actually changed since last week. Amandeep couldn't name anything; she just said, "Everything."
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked tired, and her jaw was tight all week.

qa.q: What did Amandeep walk into on the way to the Mall Road?
qa.a: She walked into a lamp post.

qa.q: How did Amandeep seem to feel during the holiday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Amandeep seemed tired and worried, with her jaw tight all week and saying the world is falling apart, though she could not name anything that had changed.

qa.q: How could Nani's question help Amandeep, and what small step might follow?
qa.a: Asking what had actually changed shows that her fear has grown without new facts; a small step would be to put the phone away for moments like the first snowfall.

qa.q: What was the holiday like for Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika spent it watching Amandeep's head bent over the phone, missing shared moments like the snow, and seems worried about Amandeep's tight jaw.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking bad news and negative posts and deciding the world is falling apart, while real information does not change.

passage:
Week 1, Monday: Manjula, twenty, joined a neighbourhood alert group for her area of Mysuru. That night she read about a chain-snatching two streets away and a stray dog chasing a cyclist. She shared both with Shreya. "Did you know it's this bad here?"
Week 2, Friday: She now checked the group before bed, again at two in the morning, and first thing at dawn. Most posts were the same three incidents, reposted and argued over. She stopped her evening walk to the lake and asked Shreya to come with her even to the vegetable shop.
Week 4, Wednesday: Shreya asked, "How many new incidents this month, actually?" Manjula scrolled for a long time. "Two, maybe. But it feels like a hundred." Her hands were cold. She put the phone face down, and five minutes later picked it up again.

qa.q: How many new incidents did Manjula find that month?
qa.a: "Two, maybe."

qa.q: Why does the neighbourhood feel so dangerous to Manjula when she can only find two incidents?
qa.a: Reading the same bad posts again and again, day and night, makes the danger feel constant, so her fear keeps rising even though the real news hardly changes.

qa.q: What turning point came in Week 4, and what could Manjula do with it?
qa.a: Shreya's question showed that "a hundred" was really two; Manjula could set fixed times to check, or leave the group, and slowly go back to her lake walk with Shreya.

qa.q: What is it like for Shreya over these weeks?
qa.a: Shreya goes from getting shocked messages to being needed for trips to the vegetable shop, and seems worried enough to finally ask a careful question.

grounding: It shows a young adult repeatedly checking negative posts and concluding her area is far worse than it is, while distress rises and real information does not.

passage: Between customers at the family hardware shop in Nabha, Zubin kept his phone under the counter, scrolling a district news page. Chain snatching in Patiala. A theft near the bus stand. A road accident on the highway. By evening he was sure the town had turned dangerous. When Simran came in, he said, "You're not walking to college alone any more. Did you see what's happening?" Simran took the phone and scrolled. "Zubin, this is the whole district. And look at the dates, some are from March." "It's still a lot." "Has anything happened on our road?" He thought. Nothing had, not in years. Simran handed the phone back. "You've been reading this since morning. You look more tired than scared." Zubin put the phone in the drawer and rubbed his eyes.

qa.q: Where did Zubin keep his phone while he scrolled?
qa.a: He kept it under the counter at the family hardware shop.

qa.q: Why did Zubin become so sure the town was dangerous?
qa.a: Zubin felt alarmed and protective, because a whole day of bad stories piled up in his mind and felt like a picture of his own town.

qa.q: What question from Simran helped Zubin check the fear?
qa.a: Asking whether anything had happened on their road, after pointing out that the stories covered the whole district and some were months old.

qa.q: How might Simran feel about suddenly being told not to walk alone?
qa.a: Simran might feel annoyed at losing freedom over old news from across the district, but also cared for.

grounding: Shows a young man scrolling bad news all day and concluding his town is dangerous, while his real information stays the same.

passage: In her dorm room in Toronto, Dalia had meant to check the weather. Two hours later she was still scrolling: wildfires, a drought, a species declared gone, a video of melting ice with sad music. Her essay sat open and untouched. When Amara knocked to walk with her to the dining hall, Dalia didn't move. "What's the point of an essay? It's all over anyway." Amara sat on the bed. "What did you learn in the last two hours that you didn't know at lunch?" Dalia opened her mouth, then closed it. Nothing new. Just the same stories, louder. Amara took the phone gently and set it on the desk. "Come eat. Then you can read one proper article, not a hundred clips." Dalia pulled on her boots, her chest still tight, but moving.

qa.q: What had Dalia meant to check before she started scrolling?
qa.a: Dalia had meant to check the weather.

qa.q: Why did Dalia feel that nothing was worth doing?
qa.a: Dalia felt anxious and hopeless because two hours of wildfires, droughts and sad videos made everything seem lost, even though she learned nothing new.

qa.q: What did Amara suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Come and eat, then read one proper article instead of a hundred clips, so Dalia stays informed without the endless feed raising her distress.

qa.q: How might Amara have felt finding Dalia like that?
qa.a: Amara was probably concerned and gentle, wanting to pull her friend out of the scroll without dismissing the worry.

grounding: Shows a young adult scrolling bad news for hours and concluding everything is hopeless while learning nothing new.

passage: In the girls' hostel at the Delhi university, Chandrika had started checking the news app every hour. Floods in one state, a train accident in another, a scam, a heatwave warning. At night she lay in bed scrolling until two, her heart racing. "Everything is falling apart," she told her roommate Anjali at breakfast, tired and pale. "The world is getting worse and worse." Anjali asked, "What good news did you read this week?" Chandrika stared at her. "None." "Nothing? Not the new metro line, or the village schools that got solar lights, or your own cousin's result?" Chandrika hadn't looked. The warden, passing by, suggested she keep her phone outside the room at night and talk to the college counsellor if the worry didn't ease. That night Chandrika left her phone on the corridor charging shelf. She slept until seven.

qa.q: Until what time did Chandrika scroll at night?
qa.a: Until two.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling at breakfast?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exhausted, convinced the world was falling apart because she only read bad news.

qa.q: What helped Chandrika, and what could she keep doing?
qa.a: Anjali asking about good news and the warden's advice to keep the phone outside at night; she can limit scrolling and talk to the counsellor if the worry stays.

qa.q: How does Anjali see the news?
qa.a: Anjali sees both bad and good news, like the new metro line and solar lights, so the world doesn't look as dark to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult doomscrolling bad news and concluding the world is getting worse, as distress rises without better information.

passage:
Dear Sahil,
You asked why I've been so quiet lately. I think it's the news. Every night since March, I read everything bad: wars, floods, crime, layoffs. I go to sleep feeling like the whole world is burning and there's no point in anything. I'm tired all the time.
Yesterday I did an experiment my professor suggested. I counted the stories I read in one evening. Forty-two. Thirty-nine were bad. And I realised I didn't know anything new at the end. I was just more scared.
So I'm trying something. News once, in the morning, from one source. No phone after ten. And I'll see the college counsellor this Friday, because the heavy feeling hasn't gone.
Write back? Tell me something good from your side.
Lavanya

qa.q: How many of the forty-two stories were bad?
qa.a: Thirty-nine were bad.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling every night since March?
qa.a: Lavanya felt hopeless and exhausted, as if the whole world were burning and nothing mattered.

qa.q: What is Lavanya trying now, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Reading the news once in the morning from one source, no phone after ten, and seeing the counsellor, because scrolling raised distress without adding real information.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sahil might feel worried for Lavanya but glad Lavanya is taking steps and asking for something good.

grounding: A young adult's letter shows doomscrolling bad news and concluding the world is worse, as distress grows without new information.

passage: Ganga, I have to tell you what happened to me this month. So, I'm Urmila, right, and I got into this habit. Every night, bed, phone, news. Accident, fire, scam, heatwave, some war. And the comments below were even worse. I'd scroll for two, three hours. By the end of the month I honestly believed nothing good was happening anywhere. I stopped going out. I felt this constant tight feeling in my chest. Then my cousin, who's a nurse, sat me down and asked me what I had actually learned from all that scrolling. I couldn't name one useful thing. I was just more frightened. She helped me delete the news apps from my phone and put one weekly news summary on my laptop. And she made me promise to talk to a counsellor if the tightness stays. It's been a week. It's a bit better.

qa.q: How long did Urmila scroll each night?
qa.a: Two, three hours.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling by the end of the month?
qa.a: Urmila felt frightened and hopeless, with a constant tight chest, believing nothing good was happening anywhere.

qa.q: What did Urmila's cousin help with, and why did it make sense?
qa.a: Deleting the news apps and keeping one weekly summary, plus a promise to see a counsellor if the tightness stays, because scrolling added fear, not knowledge.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel hearing Urmila's story?
qa.a: Ganga might feel concerned, and perhaps recognise the same habit in herself.

grounding: A young adult describes doomscrolling bad news and concluding the world is worse, with distress rising while real information does not.

passage:
Sunday. Binita lay in her hostel bed until 2 a.m., scrolling: a train accident, a robbery in the next city, a video of a flood, a thread about how everything was getting worse. Each post made her want to check the next one. When she finally slept, her heart was still racing.
Wednesday. At breakfast she told Ira, "The world is falling apart. Crime is everywhere now." Ira asked, "Is it more than last year?" Binita opened her mouth, then realised she had no idea. She had seen forty scary posts and zero numbers.
Saturday. Binita had set her phone to lock the news app at ten. With Ira she looked up the city's yearly crime report: some things were worse, several were better, most were about the same. She still cared about the flood and gave to the relief fund. But she fell asleep at eleven for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: Until what time did Binita scroll on Sunday?
qa.a: Binita lay in her hostel bed scrolling until 2 a.m.

qa.q: Why did each post make Binita want to check the next one?
qa.a: Binita felt anxious and on edge, and the bad news grabbed her attention so strongly that stopping felt impossible.

qa.q: What two changes helped Binita by Saturday?
qa.a: Locking the news app at ten and checking the city's yearly crime report with Ira, which gave real information instead of more scary posts.

qa.q: How does Ira see Binita's claim that the world is falling apart?
qa.a: Ira is gently doubtful and asks whether it is really more than last year, which prompts Binita to check.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose late-night scrolling of bad news convinces her the world is worse than it is, until she checks real figures.

passage:
Sunaina, put the phone down for a minute. When I was twenty, we had no phones, but I did the same thing with the radio. That was the year of the big floods in our state. I'm your Thomas Uncle, and I listened to every bulletin: morning, noon, midnight. Deaths, broken bridges, a boat overturned. I stopped going to college. I told your grandmother the whole world was drowning, that nothing good would ever happen again.
One evening our old neighbour, the postmaster, sat me down. "Thomas, how many letters do you think I delivered this week?" I didn't know. "Four hundred. Weddings, exam results, babies born. The radio reads out the bridges. It never reads out the babies."
I still cared about the floods; I went and helped at the relief camp. But after that, I switched the radio off at night.

qa.q: How many letters did the postmaster say were delivered that week?
qa.a: The postmaster said four hundred letters were delivered that week.

qa.q: Why did Thomas stop going to college that year?
qa.a: Thomas felt frightened and hopeless, hearing only bad news on every bulletin, until it seemed the whole world was drowning.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed things for Thomas, and why?
qa.a: The postmaster's question about letters showed that good news was happening too, just never read out, so Thomas balanced the picture.

qa.q: How might the postmaster have seen Thomas at the time?
qa.a: The postmaster likely saw a worried young person lost in the bulletins and wanted to show the ordinary good the radio left out.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a year of constant bad-news bulletins that made the world seem worse than it was.

passage:
With final exams a week away and the hostel wi-fi dropping every hour, Nazia still found time to scroll. Layoff posts. "Nobody's hiring freshers this year." A thread of rejected graduates. A video of a man crying in his car.
By Thursday she was sure there were no jobs anywhere. She couldn't concentrate on thermodynamics. What was the point?
Siddharth found her in the reading room staring at her phone instead of her notes. He pulled up the placement cell's report on his laptop. "Last year, seventy-one percent of our batch got offers. Lower than before, yes. But seventy-one."
Nazia blinked. "The posts made it sound like zero."
"Posts come from people with bad news. The ones who got jobs are busy at work."
She zipped her phone into her bag and opened her notes. The worry didn't vanish. But it shrank to a size she could study next to.

qa.q: What percentage of last year's batch got offers?
qa.a: Seventy-one percent of last year's batch got offers.

qa.q: Why was Nazia sure there were no jobs anywhere?
qa.a: Nazia felt anxious and hopeless, because days of negative posts made the worst stories feel like the whole picture.

qa.q: What helped Nazia get back to studying?
qa.a: Seeing the placement cell's real numbers with Siddharth, then zipping the phone into her bag.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the posts Nazia was reading?
qa.a: Siddharth sees them as a slice of bad news, since people who got jobs are busy at work and don't post.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose scrolling of negative posts convinces her there are no jobs, while real information says otherwise.

passage: On Diwali night, while the whole Hyderabad colony lit diyas, Aparna sat on her bed scrolling. A fire in some city. A flood somewhere else. A post saying everything was getting worse. Another saying nobody could be trusted anymore. She refreshed the feed again and again, her shoulders creeping up towards her ears. Each new headline made her chest tighter, but she couldn't stop. What if something happens to Amma on the road, she thought, though Amma was downstairs making laddoos. Her cousin Vinita knocked with a plate of sweets. "Come and see the rangoli, the kids made a peacock." "In a minute," Aparna said, not looking up. An hour later she had read forty posts and learned almost nothing new, except that she felt worse.

qa.q: What did Vinita say the kids made in the rangoli?
qa.a: A peacock.

qa.q: Why does Aparna keep refreshing the feed even as she feels worse?
qa.a: Each bad headline grabs her attention like a warning she must check, so she feels anxious and stuck, as if watching will keep everyone safe.

qa.q: What small step could help Aparna tonight?
qa.a: Put the phone away for a while, go and see the rangoli with Vinita, and check the news later from one reliable source at a set time.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when Aparna doesn't look up?
qa.a: Vinita may feel a little ignored and concerned, seeing Aparna miss the celebration while stuck on the phone.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps checking bad news and concludes the world is worse than it is, with distress rising while real information does not.
